**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** [Internal]

---

We've reached the point where our GPU fleet is saturated during working hours and idle overnight, and the question on the table is whether we should purchase additional hardware or invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the right answer is less obvious than it first appears, and I'd like us to decide it together with a shared picture of the trade-offs.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward on the surface. Our queue times during peak hours have crept from minutes to nearly an hour for larger inference jobs, and that latency is not cosmetic — it changes how people work. When a researcher has to batch their experiments to avoid the queue, iteration slows down, and slow iteration is the most expensive thing a small team pays for, even though it never appears on an invoice. Dedicated capacity would also improve reliability in a specific sense: right now a single hardware failure or a badly behaved job can degrade service for everyone, because we have so little slack. Redundancy is a form of reliability, and we currently have almost none.

But the purchase price is only the beginning of the cost. Hardware depreciates quickly in a field where model architectures and accelerator generations move fast, and our operating budget is finite in a way that makes every capital purchase an opportunity cost. Money spent on a second rack of GPUs is money not spent on engineering time, tooling, or the evaluation infrastructure several of us have argued we need. There's also a subtler point: buying capacity removes the pressure to understand our own workload. If we never have to look hard at utilisation, we never learn which of our jobs are genuinely latency-sensitive and which are just habitually run at peak times because that's when people are at their desks.

That last observation is why I lean toward the second option — improving utilisation — as our next move, with hardware purchase held in reserve rather than rejected outright. Our overnight utilisation sits near zero, and our peak is driven largely by interactive jobs that could tolerate modest queueing if we managed them intelligently. Simple scheduling changes — batching non-urgent work into off-peak windows, tiering jobs by latency sensitivity, capping concurrent large runs — could plausibly recover thirty to fifty percent of effective capacity at a cost of a few engineering weeks. That is dramatically cheaper per unit of capacity than buying it, and unlike a purchase, it's largely reversible: if the scheduler changes turn out to hurt more than they help, we roll them back and we've lost little.

Reversibility matters more than it might seem. A hardware purchase is a commitment with a horizon of years; a scheduling policy is a commitment with a horizon of weeks. When we're uncertain — and we are, because our utilisation data is patchy and self-reported — the rational move is to take the cheap, reversible step that generates information first. If we invest in better utilisation and better telemetry, we will either solve the problem or, failing that, we'll end up with precisely the data we need to size a hardware purchase correctly. Either way we win. Buying now, before we understand our own demand curve, risks spending real money on capacity that turns out to be the wrong shape — too much of one thing, not enough of another.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty in my own recommendation. There's a scenario in which our growth is real and sustained, in which case every month spent optimising is a month of friction, and the "wasted" purchase would have been fine. There's also a scenario in which a well-timed hardware grant or cloud credits materialise and change the arithmetic entirely. I don't think we can distinguish these scenarios from where we stand today, which is exactly the argument for the reversible path.

So my recommendation: spend the next six to eight weeks on scheduling, tiering, and telemetry, with a defined target — peak queue times under ten minutes. If we hit it, we've bought ourselves a year of headroom for the price of a sprint. If we miss it, we'll know exactly what to buy, how much, and why, and I'll write the purchase proposal myself with confidence rather than guesswork.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's sync.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Engineering Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more hardware or improve utilisation of what we own
**Date:** [Date]

**Summary and recommendation**

We currently run four A100-class servers at roughly 35–40% utilisation, while our queue times during peak hours have grown enough that researchers are complaining and, more worryingly, quietly working around the scheduler. The question on the table is whether to spend approximately £180k on two additional nodes or to invest six to eight weeks of engineering time in raising utilisation on the fleet we already own. My recommendation is that we do the latter first, with a defined decision point: if we cannot get sustained utilisation above 65% within one quarter, we revisit the purchase with real data in hand rather than the estimates we have now.

**The case for fixing utilisation first**

The strongest argument is simply that we don't yet know what our actual constraint is. A 35% utilisation figure sounds like slack, but utilisation numbers can be misleading — some of that idle time may be fragmentation (jobs that need a whole node sitting alongside jobs that need a fraction of one), some may be scheduling overhead, and some may be jobs that are queued behind long-running work when a smarter preemption policy would let them interleave. Until we instrument this properly, buying more hardware is a guess dressed up as a plan. The engineering work itself — better queueing, checkpoint-and-resume for preemption, job packing, and honest per-team accounting of who is holding what — is valuable regardless of what we decide later.

The cost asymmetry matters too. The £180k purchase price is only the visible part. Add power, cooling, rack space, our support contract, and the operational burden of a larger fleet, and the three-year cost of ownership is closer to £260k. Against that, the utilisation work costs us perhaps two engineers for six weeks — call it £60k of fully-loaded time — and it is largely recoverable even in the worst case, because the tooling and instrumentation we build makes any future hardware purchase work harder too.

**Latency and reliability**

It's worth being honest that utilisation improvements are not free. Pushing a cluster from 40% to 70% means jobs queue for longer and contention increases; our p99 job-start latency will likely get worse before it gets better, and we need to watch that carefully, because latency is the thing researchers actually feel. There is also a reliability dimension: checkpoint-and-resume and preemption introduce new failure modes, and a cluster running hotter has less headroom to absorb a node failure without visible impact. These are manageable risks — this is well-trodden engineering ground — but they are real, and they argue for a staged rollout rather than a big-bang change to the scheduler.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The opportunity cost cuts both ways, and we should weigh it honestly. Every week spent on scheduler work is a week not spent on the model-evaluation platform, which has its own deadline. But buying hardware also has an opportunity cost: £180k is roughly a year of a senior engineer, or the entire budget for the evaluation platform's compute needs next year. The difference is reversibility. Hardware is a largely irreversible commitment — GPUs depreciate quickly, and if our workload mix shifts (for example, if inference traffic grows faster than training, which our current trend suggests), the machines we buy today may be the wrong shape for the demand of eighteen months from now. Scheduler improvements are almost entirely reversible and, more importantly, they buy us information: after a quarter of good instrumentation, we will know whether our problem is capacity or allocation, and we can make the hardware decision with evidence.

**Uncertainty**

I want to acknowledge the genuine uncertainty here. If our workload doubles in the next six months — a plausible outcome if the new fine-tuning programme is approved — utilisation improvements will be a stopgap, and we will end up buying hardware anyway, having spent a quarter we could have spent procuring. Procurement lead times are eight to ten weeks, so "wait and see" is not free either. My proposed mitigation is to begin the procurement paperwork in parallel — approvals, quotes, budget reservation — so that if the utilisation work stalls or demand spikes, we can pull the trigger without starting from zero.

**Decision requested**

Approve the utilisation project through end of quarter, with parallel procurement preparation, and a formal go/no-go on hardware purchase at the next planning cycle. I'm happy to walk through the numbers in detail at Thursday's session.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Planning
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

---

We've reached the point in our capacity planning where the easy answers stop being adequate. Our inference cluster is running hot during business hours, batch jobs are queuing into the evening, and the question on the table is whether we should purchase additional local hardware or invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to walk through my thinking on this, because the right answer is not the obvious one, and I'd rather we argue about it now than in six months when the decision has made itself.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward and emotionally satisfying. New machines mean headroom, and headroom means we stop having conversations about why the nightly embedding refresh slipped again. But let's be honest about what we'd be buying. At current pricing, the capital outlay for a meaningful expansion would consume most of our hardware budget for the year, and that's before power, cooling, and the operational tax of managing more physical footprint. More importantly, our own telemetry tells us something uncomfortable: our fleet sits at roughly 40% average utilisation across the week. The peaks are real, but the peaks are not the machine. We are, in effect, considering buying a second car because the first one is only a problem twice a day.

That observation points toward the less glamorous path. Improving utilisation is unglamorous precisely because it's work rather than procurement — it means smarter scheduling, batching small requests together, quantising models where quality permits, and possibly time-shifting our batch workloads into the overnight trough that currently goes mostly unused. None of this is free. Engineering time is the currency here, and every sprint spent on scheduler tuning is a sprint not spent on the product roadmap. That opportunity cost is genuine, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. But it's also bounded, reversible, and — critically — it produces knowledge. If we spend six weeks making our scheduling layer intelligent and still find ourselves capacity-constrained, we will do so with a much sharper understanding of where the true bottleneck lives, and any subsequent hardware purchase will be better targeted as a result.

Latency deserves its own moment, because it's the strongest card the "buy more" side holds. Right now, our p99 latency degrades noticeably during the afternoon peak, and no amount of clever batching fixes the fundamental physics of a queue. If we had hard latency SLAs with customers, this alone might settle the argument. We don't — not yet. Our internal users grumble, but grumbling is not a contract. What we can do is set a tripwire: if p99 latency breaches a defined threshold for a sustained period, or if a customer-facing SLA becomes imminent, the hardware conversation reopens immediately and with priority. That converts an open-ended debate into a conditional commitment, which is a much healthier thing for a team our size to hold.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I want to be careful here. More machines would give us redundancy we currently lack; a single node failure today removes a third of our capacity, which is a sobering number. But utilisation work has reliability benefits too — better queueing, graceful degradation, and the ability to shed batch load to protect interactive traffic are all resilience features, not just efficiency features. And there's a reversibility asymmetry worth naming: hardware is a one-way door. Once purchased, it depreciates whether we need it or not, and reselling specialised accelerators is a loss-making exercise. Software improvements, by contrast, are almost entirely reversible. If we build the wrong scheduling abstraction, we throw it away and we're out a few weeks. If we buy the wrong rack, we're married to it.

So my recommendation is this: spend the next quarter on utilisation, with a hard, pre-agreed latency tripwire that triggers hardware procurement if we hit it. I hold real uncertainty about whether utilisation work alone will carry us through the next growth phase — my honest guess is that it buys us two or three quarters, not two years. But buying time cheaply, while learning where the real constraint lives, is strictly better than buying capacity expensively on the strength of a hunch. Let's discuss at Monday's planning session.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

---

Over the past month we've been asked, informally but repeatedly, whether we should purchase additional local AI hardware or invest in squeezing more out of the machines we already own. This memo is my attempt to settle the question with the evidence we have, and to be honest about where the evidence runs out.

Start with the numbers we can defend. Our current fleet of eight GPU nodes runs at roughly 38% average utilisation, but that average hides a sharp diurnal pattern: overnight batch training saturates the cluster, while daytime interactive work — notebooks, evaluation runs, small fine-tunes — competes for whatever is left. The result is a paradox familiar to anyone who has operated shared compute: we are simultaneously underutilised and capacity-constrained. Developers wait in queue at 2pm on a cluster that is idle at 2am. That is not a hardware problem; it is a scheduling and visibility problem, and it is the strongest argument against buying anything right now.

The cost picture reinforces this. A new node of comparable spec would cost approximately £180k upfront, plus perhaps £15k annually in power, cooling, and maintenance, and it would depreciate quickly in a market where hardware generations arrive every eighteen months. Against that, the proposed improvements — a proper job scheduler, per-team quotas, checkpointing so long jobs can be preempted, and better telemetry so we can actually see where capacity goes — represent maybe six weeks of one engineer's time. Even if we value that engineer's time generously, the utilisation path is an order of magnitude cheaper. The opportunity cost matters too: the engineers who would procure, rack, and integrate new hardware are the same people we need for the model-serving work scheduled this quarter. Buying hardware doesn't just spend money; it spends the scarcest resource we have, which is focused engineering attention.

Latency is the one place where new hardware genuinely wins, and it deserves a fair hearing. Interactive development on a contended cluster is frustrating in a way that scheduling improvements only partially fix — a queue that moves faster is still a queue. If our goal were sub-second inference at the edge, or guaranteed single-tenant performance for latency-sensitive experiments, more hardware would be the right answer. But most of our daytime contention is for batch-ish workloads that can tolerate minutes of delay, not milliseconds. A scheduler that lets a small evaluation run preempt a checkpointed training job solves the actual pain without adding a single watt to the machine room.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I want to be careful here. More nodes would give us redundancy: today, the failure of one machine removes a quarter of our training capacity, and we have no spare. That is a real risk. But it is a risk we could address more cheaply by improving our checkpointing and job-restart discipline, so that a node failure costs hours rather than days. Redundancy through better software is cheaper than redundancy through steel, and it has the side benefit of making us resilient regardless of what hardware we eventually own.

Then there is reversibility, which I think is the decisive consideration. Six weeks of scheduling and telemetry work is almost entirely recoverable: even if we later conclude we do need more hardware, the scheduler, the quotas, and the visibility tooling remain valuable on a larger fleet. Buying a node is the opposite. It is a large, largely irreversible commitment of capital to a guess about future demand — and our demand forecasts for next year range from "flat" to "triple," which is another way of saying we don't know. When you are uncertain, you want the option that preserves your ability to change course. Utilisation work preserves it; hardware purchases spend it.

So my recommendation is clear: spend the next six to eight weeks on utilisation — scheduler, quotas, preemption, telemetry — and defer the hardware decision until we have real data from a well-run cluster. If, after that, utilisation sits above 70% and queues are still painful, we buy, and we'll buy with confidence rather than anxiety.

The honest caveat: I may be wrong about how much of our contention is schedulable. If the telemetry work reveals that daytime demand is genuinely inelastic, the case for hardware strengthens considerably, and we should revisit this in Q3 rather than defending this memo out of pride.

Comments welcome by end of next week.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more hardware or improve utilisation of what we own
**Date:** Internal draft

---

We've reached the point where our inference workloads are bumping against the limits of the hardware we own, and the question in front of us is whether the right response is to buy more machines or to get more out of the ones we have. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the two options are not symmetric in cost, risk, or reversibility, and I think the framing matters as much as the answer.

Start with the economics. Our current fleet sits at roughly 45–55% utilisation across the week, but that average hides the real problem: utilisation peaks near saturation during business hours and collapses overnight and on weekends. Buying more hardware would cost us something on the order of $180K upfront plus power, cooling, and rack space, and it would be spent to solve a problem that only exists for about thirty hours a week. That's an expensive way to buy headroom. By contrast, the utilisation work — better batching, a proper queueing layer, quantisation where quality permits, and scheduling batch jobs into the overnight trough — is mostly engineering time we'd be spending anyway, plus perhaps $15K for tooling and observability. The opportunity cost cuts both ways, of course: every week engineers spend tuning schedulers is a week they're not shipping product features. But the utilisation work is bounded. I'd estimate six to eight weeks of focused effort, not an open-ended project, and the skills and tooling it builds (real per-model cost accounting, queue visibility) pay dividends regardless of what we decide later.

Latency is the strongest argument for buying hardware, and I want to take it seriously. Right now our p95 latency degrades noticeably during peak hours, and interactive users feel that. If we simply squeezed harder without adding capacity, we'd risk trading tail latency for utilisation, which is a bad trade for a product people interact with directly. But this is an argument against naive squeezing, not against utilisation work generally. A queueing layer with sensible SLOs lets us protect interactive traffic while filling spare capacity with batch and offline work. If, after that, peak-hour latency is still unacceptable, that's the moment to buy — and we'll buy with much better information about what we actually need.

Reliability cuts in an interesting direction. More machines means more redundancy, and our current setup has uncomfortable single-points-of-failure: losing one node during peak takes a meaningful chunk of capacity with it. I don't want to minimise that. But adding hardware to solve a reliability problem is the bluntest instrument available. Most of the reliability gain we need — graceful degradation, draining workloads before maintenance, failover for the serving layer — comes from software we haven't written yet, and that software is part of the same utilisation effort. Buying machines before building it would mean the new hardware inherits the same fragility.

The reversibility question is, to me, the decisive one. Hardware we buy is hardware we own: it depreciates, it consumes power whether we use it or not, and unwinding the purchase means writing off capital. Engineering effort, once spent, produces durable capability even if the specific project fails. If we invest in utilisation and it turns out our workloads grow fast enough to justify more hardware anyway, nothing is wasted — the scheduling and observability layers make the new hardware cheaper to run. If we buy hardware and our workloads plateau, we're carrying idle capital for years. One path keeps our options open; the other forecloses them.

So my recommendation is clear: do the utilisation work first, with a hard timebox and explicit success criteria. Specifically, I'd propose we target 70% sustained utilisation and p95 latency at or below current peak-hour levels within one quarter, and commit to revisiting the hardware question immediately after with real data in hand. If we hit those targets, we've likely deferred a purchase by a year or more. If we miss them, we'll know precisely which constraint — peak capacity, memory, interconnect — is binding, and we can buy exactly what's needed rather than guessing.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. My utilisation estimates come from coarse metrics, not per-model profiling, and it's possible the overnight trough is less fillable than it looks, or that batch workloads are smaller than we think. Growth is the other wildcard: if the product team's roadmap implies a doubling of inference demand next quarter, the calculus shifts toward buying sooner. I'd ask the product leads to share their demand forecast before we commit.

My suggestion for this week: approve two engineers for a one-week profiling spike, and reconvene with numbers rather than intuitions.
